name: Documented income earned in China — buy USD, one wire
fits: The RMB is your own lawful current-account income from China (salary, fees, rent received, etc.) and you can document its source and tax handling.
limit: No amount ceiling in Art. 59. The bank must see ID + source materials with transaction amounts, including tax evidence.
pros: Standard route for a foreign passport holder; whole amount in one wire; lowest conversion cost of any RMB route (tied).
cons: Fails without source/tax documents. Any unpaid Chinese tax on the income must be settled first — that, not the wire, is the large number.
tax: No tax on the conversion itself in any source read. Chinese IIT on the underlying income if unpaid: comprehensive 3%–45%, flat categories 20%.

name: Change back unused RMB with the original exchange slip (兑换水单)
fits: You converted your own foreign currency into RMB, still hold the bank's exchange slip, and the RMB is unused.
limit: Up to the unused amount on the slip; slip valid 24 months from the exchange date. Without a slip: USD 500/day on ID alone (USD 1,000 at departure venues).
pros: ID + slip only; no income or tax documents; one wire.
cons: Useless for RMB earned or gifted in China, or slips older than 24 months.
tax: None identified — this is your own money changed back. U.S. §988 gain can still arise (see penalty page).

name: Wire out foreign currency already in the account — no conversion
fits: Part of the balance is already USD (or other FX), e.g. wired in from abroad and never converted.
limit: No conversion, so no spread. Bank checks still apply; exact account-rule text was read in an earlier pass, not re-fetched today (flag).
pros: Cheapest lawful route: published wire fee only.
cons: Helps only for the part already held as FX.
tax: None identified on the transfer itself.

name: Home-sale proceeds — buy USD, one wire (bank cost priced; sale tax separate)
fits: The RMB is what you received for selling residential property registered in your name.
limit: Remittance capped at the sale price minus the taxes of that sale (your share if co-owned); registered contract, registration proof and tax certificate required (operating-guide text read in an earlier pass — flag).
pros: Large amounts in one remittance with a fixed document list.
cons: Title transfer and property taxes must be completed first; the tax certificate caps the amount.
tax: Chinese IIT 20% on the gain (proceeds minus original value and reasonable costs). Other property taxes not verified in this pass.

name: Inheritance transfer (继承财产转移) — buy USD, wire after approval
fits: You inherited assets in China from a decedent whose household registration was in China.
limit: SAFE approval at the decedent's last hukou location; inheritance proof, property documents and a tax certificate required (PBOC办法 text read in an earlier pass — flag). Bank cost below assumes approval is granted.
pros: Dedicated legal route for large sums, paid to your own account in your country of residence.
cons: Approval step, document gathering and timing are not officially priced or timed — blank, flagged.
tax: A tax certificate for the estate is required. Whether China taxes the inheritance itself was not confirmed (IIT Law lists nine categories; inheritance is not one — flag). U.S.: bequest over USD 100,000 is Form 3520-reportable.

name: Emigrant property transfer (移民财产转移) — buy USD, wire after approval
fits: You formerly lived in mainland China, emigrated, and the assets pre-date emigration.
limit: SAFE approval at the former hukou location; cancelled-hukou proof and tax certificates required (read in an earlier pass — flag). Not open to someone who never held mainland residence.
pros: Dedicated route for a former resident's accumulated property; no annual quota.
cons: Heaviest paperwork of any lawful route; approval timing unpublished — blank, flagged.
tax: Tax certificates from where the property/income arose; unpaid Chinese tax must be settled first.

name: USD 50,000/year convenience amount — ID alone, one wire per year
fits: Chinese citizens, and foreign individuals holding the Foreign Permanent Resident ID. A U.S. passport alone does not qualify for buying FX (Art. 59 route F01 applies instead).
limit: USD 50,000 equivalent per person per calendar year on ID alone. Above it, documented-purpose purchase (F01) — the amount is a convenience threshold, not a cap.
pros: No source/tax documents inside the yearly amount.
cons: USD 400,000 takes 8 calendar years. Borrowing other people's amounts is prohibited (X01).
tax: None identified on the conversion itself.

status: Lawful in principle — costs not published
name: Send RMB abroad as cross-border RMB, convert offshore (CNH)
fits: Lawful current-account RMB (e.g. salary) sent as an RMB remittance and converted outside the mainland.
limit: Bank availability, document list, outbound RMB fee and offshore conversion rate: none confirmed from an official page fetched today. Every cost cell is blank.
pros: Avoids the onshore purchase step; may suit RMB the bank will remit but not convert onshore (unverified — ask the bank in writing).
cons: You still pay an offshore spread somewhere; nothing about its size is officially published. Do not treat blank as free.

name: Dividend from your own Chinese company (statutory 20% priced; treaty 10% shown separately)
fits: The money is distributable profit inside a company you own — not personal savings. F09S prices the statutory 20%; F09T prices the treaty ceiling of 10% if you qualify as a U.S.-resident beneficial owner (procedure unverified).
limit: Genuine distributable profit only; company accounts, distribution resolution and tax filing required (detail read in an earlier pass — flag).
pros: Proper route for business profit; no annual quota; one wire.
cons: By far the most expensive lawful row because the 'cost' is real income tax, not a fee. Never use it to re-label personal savings.
tax: China IIT 20% on dividends (Art. 3(3)); US–China treaty Art. 9(2) caps the charge at 10% for a qualifying resident beneficial owner. U.S. foreign-tax-credit handling needs advice — not priced.

name: Withdraw cash abroad on a mainland UnionPay debit card
fits: You hold a UnionPay debit card on the RMB account and are physically abroad.
limit: CNY 10,000 equivalent per card per day; CNY 100,000 equivalent per person per calendar year (all cards combined). Over the yearly cap: suspended that year and the next.
pros: No documents; useful for living expenses while travelling.
cons: Priced below is the BOC card fee only. The UnionPay conversion rate and the foreign ATM owner's fee are not officially published — blank, so the true cost is higher. USD 400,000 would take 27 calendar years.
tax: None identified. Cash over USD 10,000 entering the U.S. must be declared (FinCEN Form 105) — U.S. CBP page not re-fetched today (flag).

name: Carry lawfully bought USD cash out in person
fits: You first buy USD lawfully (F01/F02/F07), then carry banknotes instead of wiring.
limit: Per trip: up to USD 5,000 equivalent released directly; USD 5,000–10,000 needs a bank carrying permit; above USD 10,000 in principle not permitted.
pros: No wire or receiving-bank fee; priced below is the conversion spread only.
cons: Not a way around the document rules — the purchase still needs its route. USD 400,000 = 80 trips at USD 5,000. Theft/loss risk is yours.
tax: None identified. Entering the U.S. with over USD 10,000 (family/group combined) requires FinCEN Form 105 — CBP page not re-fetched today (flag).

name: Splitting through relatives'/friends' USD 50,000 amounts ('ants moving')
limit: SAFE watch-list management: borrowing/lending amounts to evade controls lists the person for the listing year plus two years, under strict document review thereafter.
cons: Watch list (listing year + 2 years). Organised flight of funds is punished as 逃汇: fine up to 30%, 30%–100% in serious cases, criminal liability possible.

name: Private swaps, money changers, underground banks ('I pay RMB here, you pay USD there')
limit: Private buying/selling of FX (私自买卖外汇) is prohibited by Regulation Art. 45; only licensed banks/exchange outlets may convert.
cons: Warning, confiscation of gains, fine up to 30% (30%–100% serious); criminal liability possible.

name: False documents or a false stated purpose to buy FX
limit: Illegal FX purchase (非法套汇, Art. 40); current-account business needs a genuine lawful transaction basis (Art. 12).
cons: Conversion reversed; fine up to 30% (30%–100% serious). Untrue documents alone: individual fine up to CNY 50,000 (Art. 48).

name: Carrying over USD 10,000 cash out without a permit, or into the U.S. undeclared
limit: China: above USD 10,000 needs a SAFE carrying permit, in principle not granted. U.S.: over USD 10,000 must be declared on FinCEN Form 105 (CBP page not re-fetched today — flag).
cons: China: warning, fine up to 20% of the amount (Art. 42). U.S.: seizure/forfeiture and civil/criminal penalties (unverified today — flag).

name: Buying crypto/stablecoins with RMB to move value offshore
limit: Fiat-to-virtual-currency exchange business in China is prohibited as an illegal financial activity (PBOC 2026 notice; text read in an earlier pass, not re-fetched today — flag).
cons: Activity banned outright; no legal protection for the funds (per the notice, as read earlier — flag).

name: Borrowing or lending bank cards to evade the overseas ATM cap
limit: Expressly prohibited by 汇发〔2017〕29号: no borrowing/lending cards to evade or help evade overseas cash-withdrawal controls.
cons: Punished under the Foreign Exchange Regulation; over-cap withdrawals are suspended for that year and the next.
